title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Goals
shortDescription: Why the time until a goal shapes how people usually think about saving for it.

paragraphs: Not all savings goals are the same. Saving for a new phone in four months is a very different challenge from saving for a home deposit in ten years. One of the most useful ways to organise goals is by their time horizon: how long until the money is needed.

bodySections.heading: Short-term goals
paragraphs: Short-term goals are generally those within about one to two years: a trip, a laptop, wedding costs, a course fee, or a household appliance. Because the deadline is close, the main priority is usually certainty. The money needs to be there, in full, when the time comes.

For short-term goals, people typically focus on steady contributions and on keeping the money in a stable, accessible place. There is little time to recover from any drop in value, so predictability tends to matter more than growth.

bodySections.heading: Medium-term goals
paragraphs: Between roughly two and five years sit medium-term goals, such as a car, a home renovation, or a large family event. These goals allow more flexibility. A monthly plan can make even large amounts manageable, and there is some room to adjust the timeline if circumstances change.

bodySections.heading: Long-term goals
paragraphs: Long-term goals are further than about five years away: a home, children's education, or financial security later in life. Time is the defining advantage here. Small, regular amounts have many years to accumulate, and the effect of compounding, where growth builds on earlier growth, becomes much more significant over long periods.

Because the money is not needed soon, long-term savings can in principle ride out temporary ups and downs. This is why discussions of long-term goals often mention growth and inflation, while discussions of short-term goals focus on stability.

bodySections.heading: Breaking a goal into monthly steps
paragraphs: A simple calculation makes any goal more concrete: divide the target amount by the number of months remaining. For example, a goal of EGP 24,000 in 12 months works out to EGP 2,000 a month. The same EGP 24,000 over 24 months would be EGP 1,000 a month.

This arithmetic often reveals whether a goal is realistic as planned, or whether the timeline or the target needs adjusting. Long-term goals can be broken into yearly milestones in a similar way, which makes them feel less distant.

bodySections.heading: Balancing several goals at once
paragraphs: Most people have more than one goal running at the same time. A common approach is to give each goal its own name and target, even if the money sits together, so progress on each is visible. Some people prioritise an emergency cushion first, then split additional savings between near and distant goals according to what matters most to them.
Keeping short-term and long-term money mentally separate can prevent a common problem: dipping into long-term savings for short-term wants, which quietly delays the bigger goals.

bodySections.heading: Reviewing goals over time
paragraphs: Goals change as life changes. A goal that was long-term eventually becomes short-term as its date approaches, and the way it is approached may shift accordingly. Reviewing goals once or twice a year helps keep them aligned with current priorities and circumstances.
